diagnostic_evidence.quote: there exists a direction $a = (a_1, \ldots, a_m)^\top$ supported on $\text{supp}_{\delta}(q^{*}_n)$ such that $\sum_{i\in [m]}\frac{a_i}{\sigma^2(x_i)}R_iR^\top_i = 0$

issues.failure_explanation: The linear dependence of the matrices $R_iR_i^T/\sigma^2(x_i)$ provides a direction $a$ with $\sum a_i R_iR_i^T/\sigma^2(x_i)=0$ supported on supp_δ, but the perturbation $q^*_n+ta$ stays in the probability simplex $\mathcal{P}_m$ only if $\sum a_i=0$. The linear dependence does not imply $\sum a_i=0$, so the perturbation may leave $\mathcal{P}_m$. A nontrivial case-split argument is needed: if $\sum a_i\neq 0$, one can construct a feasible point with strictly smaller objective (contradicting optimality), forcing $\sum a_i=0$ at any optimal solution and enabling the perturbation.

failure_location.quote: Applying a perturbation argument for $q^*_n$ along $a$ yields another optimal solution that has a smaller $\delta$-support.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Supply the missing case-split argument: show that if a null direction $a$ has $\sum a_i\neq 0$, then $q^*$ cannot be optimal (construct $q'=(q^*-sa/(\sum a_i))/(1-s)$ with $H(q')<H(q^*)$), so at optimality all null directions satisfy $\sum a_i=0$ and the perturbation preserves feasibility.
issues.overall_effect: The sparsity bound $|\text{supp}_\delta(q_n^*)|\leq(n^2+n)/2$ in equation (spt) is not established by the given proof. The convexity and existence of a minimizer (used by Lemma lm:a2 and Theorem thm:main) are separately proven and remain intact.
issues.title: Incomplete perturbation argument in sparsity proof of Lemma mkjh
issues.why_classification: The gap requires a contained but nontrivial argument (case analysis on the sum of perturbation coefficients) that is not routine algebra. Fixing it preserves the stated sparsity bound and all downstream results, without requiring new global proof architecture.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: the second uses the Gauss--Markov theorem

issues.failure_explanation: The Gauss–Markov theorem gives H ≤ MSE_OLS (the trace of the ordinary least-squares covariance), not H ≤ G. Here G = tr(V^T W^{1/2}Σ W^{1/2}V) is not the OLS covariance trace; the OLS covariance trace is tr((V^TWV)^{-1}G_matrix(V^TWV)^{-1}), which satisfies MSE_OLS ≤ ‖(V^TWV)^{-1}‖²·G. In fact, when Σ = I and the Christoffel weight gives tr(V^TWV) = n always, the AM–HM inequality yields H = tr((V^TWV)^{-1}) ≥ n = tr(V^TWV) = G, with equality iff V^TWV = I. So the claimed inequality H ≤ G is reversed in general (H ≥ G when Σ = I and V^TWV ≠ I), even on event 𝒜 where Λ(V^TWV) ⊆ [0.81, 1.21].

failure_location.quote: $H(\bm q^{*}_n)\leq H(\bm p^*_n)\leq G(\bm p^*_n)$ (the first inequality follows from the definition of $\bm q_n^*$ and the second uses the Gauss--Markov theorem), which implies $\E_\XX[H(\bm q^{*}_n)]\leq \E_\XX[G(\bm p^*_n)]$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the false inequality with the correct bound H(p) ≤ ‖(V^TWV)^{-1}‖²·G(p) (from Gauss–Markov combined with equation (eq1)), noting that on 𝒜 this gives H ≤ (1/0.81)G. Adjust the qualitative comparison accordingly: the reweighted method's variance is comparable to (not strictly less than) the non-reweighted quantity G.
issues.overall_effect: The remark's conclusion that the reweighted estimator has lower estimation variance (E[H(q*_n)] ≤ E[G(p*_n)]) is unsupported and sometimes reversed. The qualitative argument that HLS-2 reduces variance at the cost of bias is not established by this comparison. Formal error bounds in Theorem thm:main are unaffected since they bound H and G separately.
issues.title: False inequality H(p*) ≤ G(p*) attributed to Gauss–Markov in Remark rem:compare
issues.why_classification: The false inequality is a substantive mathematical claim supporting the paper's interpretation of the reweighted method's advantage. The fix requires replacing the comparison with a different (weaker but correct) bound and reinterpreting the qualitative conclusion. No formal theorem changes, but a substantive interpretive promise (strict variance reduction) must be withdrawn or weakened.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Choosing $l\geq \log(1/\delta)/\log 2$ and noting $2/\log 2<3$ yields the desired result.
if $n> 10\log (1/\delta) k$, then with probability at least $1-\delta$

issues.failure_explanation: The boosting argument partitions n basis functions into l = ⌊n/k⌋ independent groups, each failing with probability ≤ 1/2 (or ≤ 0.9 in thm:984). Achieving failure probability ≤ δ requires l ≥ log₂(1/δ). But n > 1.5·log(1/δ)·k only guarantees l = ⌊n/k⌋ ≥ ⌊1.5·log(1/δ)⌋, which can be strictly less than log₂(1/δ) = log(1/δ)/log 2 ≈ 1.443·log(1/δ) because the gap 1.5 − 1.443 ≈ 0.057 is smaller than the floor loss of 1. For example, at δ = 0.05 the condition gives l ≥ 4 but log₂(20) ≈ 4.32 requires l ≥ 5, so the achieved probability is only ≥ 1 − (1/2)^4 = 0.9375 < 0.95. The same floor issue affects thm:984 for large δ.

failure_location.quote: if $k = \lceil2\e^{-2}\|\sigma\|^2_{L^2_\mu}\rceil$ and $n> 1.5\log(1/\delta)k$, where $\sigma^2(x) = \mathrm{Var}[g(x, Z)| x]$, then with probability at least $1-\delta$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Increase the constant in the lower bound on n to account for the floor: e.g., require n > (1.5·log(1/δ) + 1)·k in thm:rb (or use constant 2 instead of 1.5), and analogously adjust the constant 10 in thm:984. This preserves the log(1/δ) scaling and all substantive guarantees.
issues.overall_effect: The probability guarantees 1−δ in both Theorem thm:rb and Theorem thm:984 are slightly overstated. The approximation rates (ε and 24√(rτ_{r+1})) and the scaling of n in terms of log(1/δ) are preserved; only the precise confidence level is off by a constant factor in the failure probability.
issues.title: Boosting conditions in Theorems thm:rb and thm:984 fail to achieve stated probability due to integer group count
issues.why_classification: A short, local change to the constants in the theorem statements (adding 1 to the lower bound on n or increasing the multiplicative constant) fully resolves the floor discrepancy and preserves every substantive claim and guarantee, with no new lemma or construction needed.
